notes.text: Nepali puts the verb last. Ma bhat khanchu is literally I rice eat. Rearrange, and it clicks.
Namaste is one word for hello, goodbye, morning and night. Add -skar for namaskar when you want extra respect.
Three words mean you: ta for children, timi for friends, tapai for everyone else. Pick wrong and people notice.
Your father's elder brother is thulo buwa, big father. His younger brother is kaka. Age decides the word.
Khana means both food and rice, because dal bhat is the meal. Asking khana khanu bhayo means did you eat.
Counting stops being regular fast: every number to a hundred has its own shape. Nepalis simply memorise all ninety-nine.
Rato, red, carries luck and marriage. Kalo, black, is what you say when warding off the evil eye.
Ask distances in ghanta, hours, not kilometres. In the hills a village is two hours away, never twelve kilometres.
Nepal runs its own clock, fifteen minutes off India. Bikram Sambat calendar too, running about fifty-seven years ahead.
Kati ho asks the price; kati parcha asks what it costs you. Vendors expect the follow-up: ali kam garnus.
Nepali says dukhyo, it hurt, in past tense for pain happening now. Tauko dukhyo means my head aches.
Shoes come off at the door, and so does the word ghar. Ghar means house, family and homeland together.
Kaam is work, but jagir is a salaried job. Families ask about jagir, because that one means security.
Feelings sit in the liver, not the heart. Maya lagyo, love struck me, arrives at you rather than from you.
During Dashain elders press rice tika onto your forehead. You do not say thanks, you bow and touch feet.
